passages.original: muros urbis Romae sic ampliavit, ut quinquaginta prope milia murorum eius ambitus teneant, idem quadruplatores ac delatores ingenti severitate persecutus est. tabulas publicas ad privatorum securitatem exuri in Foro Traiani semel iussit, amnestia etiam sub eo delictorum publicorum decreta est de exemplo Atheniensium, cuius rei etiam Tullius in Philippicis meminit, fures provinciales repetundarum ac peculatus reos ultra militarem modum est persecutus, ut eos ingentibus suppliciis cruciatibusque puniret. in Templo Solis multum auri gemmarumque constituit. cum vastatum Illyricum ac Moesiam deperditam videret, provinciam Transdanuvinam Daciam a Traiano constitutam sublato exercitu et provincialibus reliquit, desperans eam posse retineri, abductosque ex ea populos in Moesia conlocavit appellavitque eam Daciam, quae nunc duas Moesias dividit.
passages.english: He enlarged the walls of the city of Rome so that their circuit extends nearly fifty miles. He also pursued informers and denouncers with great severity. He once ordered the public records to be burned in the Forum of Trajan for the security of private persons. An amnesty for public offences was also decreed under him, on the model of the Athenians, which Tullius also mentions in the Philippics. He pursued provincial thieves, and those accused of extortion and embezzlement, beyond the military measure, punishing them with enormous penalties and tortures. In the Temple of the Sun he placed much gold and many gems. When he saw Illyricum laid waste and Moesia lost, he abandoned the province of Dacia across the Danube, which Trajan had established, withdrawing the army and the provincials, since he despaired of being able to hold it. He settled the peoples brought out of it in Moesia and called it Dacia, which now divides the two Moesias.
passages.notes: 'quinquaginta prope milia' is presumably fifty miles (milia passuum), a figure far greater than the actual circuit of the Aurelian Walls (about 12 miles). 'ultra militarem modum' is literally 'beyond the military measure', i.e. with more than military severity. 'Tullius' is Cicero, who mentions the Athenian amnesty in the First Philippic.
